note.explanation: To round a number to a given number of significant figures, keep the required digits and use the next digit to decide whether to change the last kept digit. If the next digit is 5, use the rule in your textbook: an odd last kept digit goes up by one, while an even one stays the same.
examples: 3.4567 × 10⁴ kg rounded to 3 significant figures is 3.46 × 10⁴ kg.
4.45 × 10² m rounded to 2 significant figures is 4.4 × 10² m.
note.simple: Keep the digits you need. Look at the next digit to decide what happens to the last digit you keep.
note.checkQuestion: Round off to 2 significant figures: 4.55 × 10² m.
note.title: Rounding off to significant figures
steps: Choose how many significant figures to keep.
Look at the first digit that will be left out.
If it is greater than 5, increase the last kept digit by 1; if it is less than 5, keep it unchanged.
If the digit is exactly 5, use the odd/even rule given in your textbook.
Write the rounded number with its original power of ten and unit.

examTips: A board question may ask you to round a measurement to a stated number of significant figures; show which digit is retained and use the next digit to justify the change.
For an exact 5, state whether the last retained digit is odd or even and apply the rule from your textbook.
Keep the power of ten and the unit unchanged when rounding a number written in scientific notation.
Write the final answer clearly with the requested number of significant figures; a correct value with an unclear or incorrect power of ten can lose marks.

explain.title: Keep the requested significant figures
explain.body: Significant figures are the accurately known digits and first doubtful digit in any measurement. When rounding, keep the number of significant figures asked for, then inspect the next digit.

explain.title: Digits below or above 5
explain.body: Your textbook says: “If the last digit is more than 5, the retained digit is increased by one and if it is less than 5, it is retained as such.” So a next digit of 1, 2, 3 or 4 leaves the last kept digit unchanged; a next digit of 6, 7, 8 or 9 increases it by one.

explain.title: When the next digit is exactly 5
explain.body: Your textbook gives this rule: “If the number before the 5 is odd, one is added to the last digit retained. If the number before the 5 is even, it remains the same.” For example, 4.45 rounds to 4.4 at two significant figures, while 4.55 rounds to 4.6.

explain.title: Use the nearer value when needed
explain.body: Your textbook also explains that sometimes logic is applied to decide the fate of a digit. It gives 4.452 rounded to two significant figures as 4.5, because 4.452 is closer to 4.5 than to 4.4.

mistakes: Keeping too many or too few significant figures instead of the number requested.
Changing the retained digit when the next digit is less than 5.
Forgetting the odd/even rule when the next digit is exactly 5.
Changing or omitting the power of ten or the unit in the final answer.
Rounding 4.452 to 4.4 without considering the textbook's nearest-value explanation.
